newsitem.title: INDIA: India pepper exchange plans stir hopes for others.
newsitem.headline: India pepper exchange plans stir hopes for others.

text.p: India's plans to start an international pepper futures exchange in April will open the way for commodity futures trading in a country whose economy is mainly farm-based, industry officials said on Wednesday.

"It is a step in the right direction. Futures trading is the best price-risk managment system in a free market economy," Taranath Vidyasagar, President of the India Pepper and Spices Trade Association (IPSTA), told Reuters.
The Food Ministry said on Tuesday that the country's first International Pepper Futures Exchange and clearing house would start functioning in the southern state of Kerala by April.
A Food Ministry statement said a committee, set up to supervise and expedite the exchange to regulate forward trading in pepper, had on Monday approved draft guidelines for the purpose.
India's cabinet decided in the second half of 1995 to upgrade the domestic futures commodity exchange, run by IPSTA in Kochi in Kerala state into an international exchange.

"This Exchange and Clearing House will have a stabilising influence on forward trading in pepper by acting as a mechanism for ensuring steady stock on a regulated price to international buyers," the ministry statement said.

Analysts say India, which has opened its economy after decades of socialist controls, has developed cold feet on introducing comodity futures trading due to the conflicting interests of its 13-party centre-left coalition government.
They say the government could be concerned that its pro-farmer image would be damaged if market-economy measures like futures trading were introduced.

The previous Congress party government had in 1993 decided to revive futures trade, which fell into disfavour three decades ago. An official committee has recommended futures trading in cotton, oilseeds and silver, gold and sugar.
At present futures trading is allowed in castorseed, hessian, gur (jaggery), potatoes, turmeric and pepper.
Vidyasagar said the association was currently running a domestic exchange and would open a separate division for international trade.
"We are expecting a jump in volume (of pepper trade) of at least 50 percent jump in a year's time, from the present volume of (trade worth) six billion rupees ($168 million)," Vidyasagar said.
V. Jayashankar, chairman of the state-run Spices Board, said setting up of the futures exchange would over a period of time ensure better prices for domestic growers and exporters.
Jayashankar said the government's role would be to ensure that there were no artificial barriers to trade and no shortages due to speculation.
Every year India produces about one-third of the world's total pepper output of 180,000 tonnes. The other major producers include Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam.
Vidyasagar said India annually exports about 30,000 tonnes of pepper to mainly the United States, Europe and Japan. The remaining is consumed domestically.
Indians are big pepper consumers but globally the spice is used by meat packers, commercial bakers, pickle packers and condiment manufacturers.
The Food Ministry statement said it has been also proposed setting up a second trading floor for the exchange at Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia.

Vidyasagar said the association was still to decide on how to go ahead with the exchange in Malaysia. "So far in principle, we have taken a decision but we have not worked out the modalities," he said.
"It is a good augury. We are trying to get international support to start international futures exchange for castor seed and castor oil," said G.K. Shah of the Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd.
IPSTA secretary P. Sethuram said mock trading at the pepper exchange would start by March 15. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
